renewalGestationDays.citation: Median days from ovulation to birth, which the plan's conception date stands for: Jukic, Baird, Weinberg, McConnaughey and Wilcox (2013), 'Length of human pregnancy and contributors to its natural variation', Human Reproduction 28(10), Table I, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3777570/: "The median time from ovulation to birth was 268 days (38 weeks, 2 days)." Research file data/research/people/jukic-gestation-2013.json, checked by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts. Every planned pregnancy still lasts this one median (SG-M1-births-circumstances).

renewalAgeCenter.citation: Where the age term of a couple's plan is highest: the mean age of the national fertility schedule. NCHS, Births: Final Data for 2024, National Vital Statistics Reports 75(2), Table 6, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-02.pdf (United States: 12.6, 55.8, 89.5, 93.7, 54.3 and 12.7 births per 1,000 women at 15-19 through 40-44), stored for all 56 places in data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json. Derived by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts.
renewalAgeCenter.estimatedFrom: Rate-weighted mean of the five-year age groups' midpoints, ages 15 to 44: 30.0 years nationally. The places differ (28.1 to 32.1), but the plan reads one national center until the builder item people-births-age-shape-by-place reads each place's own.

spread.citation: The same mean for each of the 56 places in data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json (NCHS 2024 Table 6), lowest to highest.

renewalAgeSpread.citation: How fast the age term falls away from its center: set so the term changes sign at the ages where a normal curve fitted to the national age-specific birth rates falls to half its peak. NCHS, Births: Final Data for 2024, NVSR 75(2), Table 6, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-02.pdf, via data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json. Derived by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts.
renewalAgeSpread.estimatedFrom: Standard deviation of the 2024 national fertility schedule, ages 15 to 44, with the within-group variance of five-year groups (25/12) added: 6.13 years. The term 2exp(-d^2) - 1 with d = (age - center)/spread is zero at d = 0.83, and a normal curve is at half its peak at 1.18 standard deviations, so spread = 6.13 x 1.18 / 0.83 = 6.13 x sqrt(2) = 8.66, rounded to 8.7.

spread.citation: The same conversion for each of the 56 places in data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json (NCHS 2024 Table 6), lowest to highest.

renewalWebWeight.citation: Fitted in played years so that a full couple's choice to plan a child moves with the outcome web's birth-rate factor for the mother's own age and home about as the counted women's births do (elasticity 1). Bench worlds of four drawn places (Key Vista, Florida; Red Rock, Arizona; Camden, Alabama; Baxter, Iowa; place draws scratch:6 to scratch:9 on web-births-full) review 77 couples through a year, and 3 of them plan a child. Read from the couples' recorded plan scores, a factor swing of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 reaches 1, 2, 3 and 7 more couples at weight 7.5 (elasticity 3.3 to 5.8) and 0, 1, 1 and 2 more at weight 3 (elasticity 0 to 1.7, 1.1 on average). A town's year cannot resolve a response finer than a couple, so the weight rests on this pooled count. The web's factor is the place's own unemployment, home-price and abortion-law effect on births (data/research/outcome-web/links.json); never a rate on the individual.

spread.unit: score per unit of factor change
spread.citation: The pooled count's average elasticity over factor swings of 0.1 to 0.4 is 0.5 at weight 2 and 1.6 at weight 5, inside the band of 0.5 to 2. src/core2/births-full-web.test.ts follows a shifted web month row to the couples it tips, by record id.

renewalTimingPeakYears.citation: Years after the last birth (or the start of the partnership) at which the timing pull toward another child is strongest: the national median interpregnancy interval. NCHS Data Brief No. 240 (Thoma, Copen and Kirmeyer, 2016), https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db240.htm: "The median interpregnancy interval was 24–29 months, or 2–2.5 years." Research file data/research/people/nchs-db240-interpregnancy-2014.json, checked by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts.
renewalTimingPeakYears.estimatedFrom: The middle of the published median band, 24 up to 30 months: 27 months, 2.25 years. The interval runs from a birth to the next conception, the same clock the plan's timing term reads.

spread.unit: years from a birth to the next conception
spread.citation: The brief's own band for the median, 2 to 2.5 years (2014 second and higher-order singleton births, 47 states and DC).

renewalIncomeWeight.citation: PW-8: weight on household job income against the place's median, as the bounded ratio (r - 1)/(r + 1), so no income at all costs at most this weight (it was a log cliff of -15.9 at $0). Direction from the literature on income and fertility timing; no rates enter actors.

spread.citation: Checked against the town's yearly births and the full couples' decisions in two fresh played-world seeds; 2 keeps a median-income couple at the old log weight's slope near the median. Oct 24 2026 (pool item people-births-over-state-rate-small-town): raised to the top of this range with the savings and partnership terms centered, so a couple's yearly births track the state's 2024 rate for the women in town (NCHS NVSR 75(2) Table 6, via data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json) in M1-09's half-year check; a total check, never an input to one couple's choice.

renewalMedianAnnualIncomeMinor.citation: The area median family income a place with no HUD row is read against: what the places with a row read. HUD FY2025 Section 8 income limits (very low limit for a family of four, src/core2/reference/town-rent.generated.ts; methodology https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/il.html), each limit times renewalMedianPerVeryLowLimit, weighted by each HUD area's population. Derived by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts.
renewalMedianAnnualIncomeMinor.estimatedFrom: Population-weighted median of twice the very low limit over the 4,763 HUD county and New England town areas: $109,000. It replaces the Census household median of $80,610 the old engine ported, which was a different measure from the family median every other place reads. HUD's own national median page could not be read from the cloud (an empty response with status 202).

spread.citation: The population-weighted 25th and 75th percentiles of the same areas, $93,900 to $125,900.

renewalMedianPerVeryLowLimit.citation: HUD income limits: the very low-income limit for a family of four is 50% of the area median family income (HUD Income Limits methodology, https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/il.html). The place's own HUD row gives its median, so the couple's income is read against what is usual where they live.

renewalJobWeight.citation: PW-8: stability of work. Each partner with a paying job adds this weight, centered on one earner. Direction: economic uncertainty and job loss delay births (Schneider 2015, Journal of Marriage and Family 77(5), 'The Great Recession, Fertility, and Uncertainty'). The size is tunable.

Oct 24 2026 (pool item people-births-over-state-rate-small-town): raised to the top of this range with the savings and partnership terms centered, so a couple's yearly births track the state's 2024 rate for the women in town (NCHS NVSR 75(2) Table 6, via data/research/renewal/natality-2024.json) in M1-09's half-year check; a total check, never an input to one couple's choice.

renewalRoomWeight.citation: PW-8: room for a child. What one more bedroom costs a year at the place's HUD fair market rents, against household income, as a bounded share. Direction: higher housing costs lower births among renters (Dettling and Kearney 2014, Journal of Public Economics 110, 'House prices and birth rates'). The size is tunable.

renewalConditionWeight.citation: PW-8: the mother's recorded chronic conditions from the health module weigh against planning a pregnancy, as a bounded share n/(n + 1). The size is tunable.

spread.citation: Checked against the full couples' decisions in two fresh played-world seeds.

renewalClosenessWeight.citation: PW-8: how close the partners are, from their relationship record (0 to 1; one half is the closeness model's midpoint), centered on that midpoint. The size is tunable.

spread.citation: Checked against the full couples' decisions in two fresh played-world seeds.

renewalUnknownCloseness.citation: PW-8: when partners have no relationship record yet, their closeness is estimated at the closeness model's midpoint (level 0.5, src/core2/closeness.ts levelFromHours), never zero.
renewalUnknownCloseness.estimatedFrom: Closeness model midpoint; the estimate weighs zero in the decision.

renewalUnionAgeYears.citation: PW-8: when a couple has no dated partner fact and no children, their start is estimated as the mother reaching the usual age of a first union. First unions for U.S. women mostly begin in the early twenties (CDC NCHS National Survey of Family Growth, first cohabitation and first marriage reports).
renewalUnionAgeYears.estimatedFrom: NSFG first-union timing for women; registered as SG-PW8-partnership-start until partnerships carry their own start date.

spread.citation: Early-twenties range of first unions; the timing term's shape is checked against it.

renewalCountedBirthSpacingDays.citation: PW-8: a counted woman whose youngest child is younger than this is not next in line for a counted birth: about six months postpartum plus a 266-day pregnancy. Births this close together are a small share of U.S. births (CDC NCHS, interpregnancy intervals, NVSS).
renewalCountedBirthSpacingDays.estimatedFrom: Short interpregnancy intervals (under six months) are uncommon; six months plus gestation.

spread.citation: Twelve to eighteen months between births; the town's yearly total is set by the rates either way.

renewalRecoveryWeight.citation: PW-8: how strongly a recent birth pulls against planning another pregnancy, as weight x exp(-days since the birth / renewalRecoveryDays). WHO recommends waiting at least 24 months after a live birth before the next pregnancy (Report of a WHO Technical Consultation on Birth Spacing, 2005). The size is tunable.

spread.citation: Checked against the played-world runs: at 6, a couple three months after a birth waits; at two years the pull is under 0.3.

renewalRecoveryDays.citation: PW-8: how fast the recovery pull fades (days for it to fall by e). Chosen so the pull has nearly faded by the WHO's recommended 24 months after a live birth (Report of a WHO Technical Consultation on Birth Spacing, 2005).
renewalRecoveryDays.estimatedFrom: WHO 24-month birth-to-pregnancy recommendation; about three e-folds by two years.

spread.citation: Two to four e-folds within the recommended 24 months.

renewalUnplannedExposure.citation: Exposure a couple that chose to wait adds each review when it has no cushion at all, scaled by the mother's age curve and the cushion; it checks the town's total and never picks a couple. Guttmacher Institute, 'Unintended Pregnancy in the United States' (fact sheet, January 2019, https://www.guttmacher.org/sites/default/files/factsheet/fb-unintended-pregnancy-us_0_4.pdf): "In 2011, there were 45 unintended pregnancies for every 1,000 women aged 15–44 in the United States. In other words, nearly 5% of reproductive-age women have an unintended pregnancy each year."
renewalUnplannedExposure.estimatedFrom: Played years in drawn towns, counting named and counted unplanned pregnancies (each counted decision times the households it stands for) per 1,000 women aged 15 to 44: seven towns gave 71.4 at 0.5; at 0.315 the same seven gave 50.7 and eight more 68.5; at 0.27 eight fresh towns gave 59.7, inside the band. Weighted by women over all four batches (23,529), the rate is about 169 per 1,000 per unit of exposure, so 45 / 169 = 0.266, rounded to 0.27; single towns run from 0 to 81, so the town's total, not one town, is what this checks.

spread.citation: The states' 2006 range scaled to the 2011 national rate: "In 2006, the median U.S. rate of unintended pregnancies was 51 per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44... The state with the highest rate of unintended pregnancies was Mississippi, 69 per 1,000 women... New Hampshire had the lowest rate, 36 per 1,000 women" (Journalist's Resource on Guttmacher, 'Unintended Pregnancy Rates at the State Level', Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health, 2011, https://journalistsresource.org/politics-and-government/u-s-state-rates-unintended-pregnancy/); 36 and 69 times 45/51 are 32 and 61 per 1,000, so 0.27 x 32/45 and 0.27 x 61/45.

renewalUnplannedAcceptance.citation: Pull toward carrying a pregnancy that has already begun, added to the circumstances a planned birth weighs.

spread.reason: Sensitivity 0 to 1.5 pending a generated-year check.

renewalTravelWeight.citation: How hard travel to a provider weighs on ending a pregnancy, scaled by distance and the household's cash.

spread.reason: Sensitivity 1 to 4 pending a generated-year check.

renewalTravelHalfMiles.citation: Miles at which travel weighs half as much as it ever will; a smooth curve, no cutoff.

renewalTravelCostPerMileMinor.citation: Cost of getting there per mile, in cents; used only to weigh the cost against her cash. IRS standard mileage rates, https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/standard-mileage-rates, 2025 row: "2025 | 70 | 14 | 21" (business, charity, medical cents per mile).

spread.citation: The IRS 2025 medical rate (driving's variable cost, what the IRS allows for travel to medical care) to its business rate (the whole cost of owning and driving a car), from the same table.

renewalTravelCostPerMileMinor.estimatedFrom: Between the IRS 2025 medical and business mileage rates, nearer the business rate for a trip far enough to need a share of lodging.
